1.text:
What Would Count as Proof?

Welcome to Deck 23 of the speculative science unit: astrobiology, covering origins, extremes and the search. In Deck 20, you asked whether life exists beyond Earth. Today we go deeper: how did life start at all, where should we look next, and how would we ever know?

Keep your Evidence Meter ready. The big question for today is: what would count as proof?

2.text:
Proof or Hint?

Sort each one: is it PROOF of alien life, or only a HINT?

A radio signal from a star that repeats in a pattern. Fossil-like spots in a rock from Mars. Oxygen and methane together in a planet's air. A living microbe in a sample from Europa. A strange object speeding through our Solar System.

Write P or H in each box. We'll re-check your sort in the exit ticket, so hold onto it.

3.text:
Today I Can...

This is your checklist. Copy these as "I can" statements and rate yourself at the end.

I can use NASA's working definition of life. I can place early life on a timeline and judge the evidence. I can explain what the Miller-Urey experiment showed. I can describe how life's building blocks form in space. I can compare RNA-first and metabolism-first ideas. I can compare places where life may have started. I can trace the carbon in my body back to stars.

I can tell the weak from the strong anthropic principle. I can describe life at the extremes. I can rank Mars, Europa, Enceladus and Titan as places to look. I can judge claims of life and of alien signals. And I can weigh answers to the Fermi paradox. These connect to Indiana standards ES.2.2, ES.4.1, ES.2.3 and ES.1.1 and NGSS Practice 7, plus some enrichment.

4.text:
Part 1: How Did Life Start?

How did life go from chemistry to biology on the early Earth? Scientists have some strong clues and some big open questions.

Keep this puzzle in mind: which came first, genes or metabolism?

5.text:
What Counts as Life?

NASA's working definition of life is a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution. It needs metabolism (it runs its own chemistry) and genes (it can evolve). ESTABLISHED FACT.

Test the definition. Fire grows and uses energy. Crystals grow and organize. Neither evolves, so neither is alive. ESTABLISHED FACT. Viruses evolve but can't copy themselves without a host cell. Are they alive? That's debated, so it's UNKNOWN.

And which came first, genes or metabolism? UNKNOWN.

Did you know? A mule can't have babies, but it's still alive. Definitions of life always have tricky cases.

6.text:
When Did Life Start?

Ga means billions of years ago. Let's walk the timeline. 4.54 Ga: Earth forms (Deck 4). ESTABLISHED FACT. About 4.2 Ga: LUCA, the last common ancestor of all life, may date to here, according to a 2024 study. It's debated, a PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

4.1 Ga: carbon in a zircon crystal "looks" like life's carbon, but it's disputed, so UNKNOWN. 3.7 to 3.8 Ga: carbon isotopes and possible stromatolites in Greenland. Debated, a PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS. About 3.5 Ga: stromatolite fossils in Western Australia, widely accepted. ESTABLISHED FACT.

Notice the pattern: the older the claim, the more debated it is. Still, the big idea holds: life showed up early, within about a billion years of Earth forming. ESTABLISHED FACT.

7.text:
Miller-Urey: Life's Parts from Sparks

In 1952, Stanley Miller and Harold Urey sparked a model early atmosphere. Methane, ammonia, hydrogen, water and sparks made amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. ESTABLISHED FACT.

In 2008, scientists re-tested Miller's saved vials and found 22 amino acids.

But early Earth's air may not have been this rich in methane and ammonia. That's debated, a PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS. And remember: it made life's building blocks without life. It did not make life. ESTABLISHED FACT.

8.text:
Building Blocks from Space

Strecker synthesis: aldehyde plus ammonia plus cyanide make amino acids with no life needed. It makes many kinds, in left- and right-handed forms. ESTABLISHED FACT. Interestingly, life uses almost only left-handed ones, and nobody knows why.

Meteorites and Bennu: the Murchison meteorite has more than 90 kinds of amino acids named. Samples from the asteroid Bennu (2025) held 14 of life's 20 amino acids and all 5 nucleobases. ESTABLISHED FACT.

Panspermia is the idea that life itself, not just ingredients, rode to Earth on rocks from another world. INFORMED SPECULATION. Even if it's true, it doesn't explain how life started in the first place.

9.text:
Genes First or Metabolism First?

There are two leading ideas for how chemistry became biology.

RNA world (genes first): RNA stores information, like DNA. RNA can copy itself and speed up reactions, as ribozymes. Mineral surfaces may help short RNA pieces grow longer. PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

Metabolism first: iron-sulfur minerals at hot vents drive the first chemistry. Iron-sulfur clusters still sit inside many enzymes today, like a leftover clue. Genes came later. PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS. It's a chicken-and-egg problem!

10.text:
Where Did Life Start?

Life needs energy, a way to concentrate ingredients and a safe place to build. Here are the candidates.

A warm little pond (Darwin's idea): volcanoes and lightning add chemicals, and the small size concentrates them. The problem is that UV light can break molecules. PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS. Deep-sea vents (black smokers): lots of heat energy and CHNOPS elements. But heat can break molecules apart. PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS. Hot springs on land: heat plus wet-dry cycles that join molecules. But that needs dry land early on. PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

Impact craters: impacts make cyanide and heat water. But impacts also destroy. PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS. Ice (a cold start): cold slows breakdown, and salty veins concentrate ingredients. But reactions are very slow. INFORMED SPECULATION.

11.text:
Made of Star Stuff

Every carbon atom in your body was made inside a star. Carbon is made in ordinary stars when 3 helium nuclei fuse, called the triple-alpha process. ESTABLISHED FACT.

Stars spread that carbon by stellar winds (red giants) and by supernovae. ESTABLISHED FACT. About half of the elements heavier than iron are made by slow neutron capture (the s-process) in aging giant stars. Most of the rest come from fast neutron capture (the r-process) in neutron-star collisions and possibly rare supernovae. ESTABLISHED FACT.

Could a planet around a first-generation star host life like ours? Probably not: there were too few heavy elements. PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

12.text:
Is the Universe Tuned for Life?

Small changes to some forces would change how stars make carbon. That's debated, a PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

Weak anthropic principle: we can only find ourselves in a universe that allows observers. So it is no surprise ours allows life. That's philosophy, INFORMED SPECULATION.

Strong anthropic principle: the universe MUST produce life to observe it. Some cite the double-slit experiment and Schrödinger's cat, but those don't need a human observer. And what counts as an observer? It's speculation, INFORMED SPECULATION.

13.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Two questions. First: the RNA world idea is supported because RNA can... A) store information, copy itself and speed up reactions, B) form cell membranes, C) make amino acids from lightning, or D) only survive at hot vents?

Second: Strecker synthesis is a non-living way to make... A) amino acids, B) nucleic acids like DNA, C) whole cells, or D) carbon atoms? Use Slides 8 and 9.

14.text:
Part 2: Where to Look

Now we explore life at the extremes, and the best places beyond Earth. Extremophiles show how tough life is, and that widens the list of places to search.

Keep this question in mind: if life can live there on Earth, could it live there out there?

15.text:
Life at the Extremes

Tardigrades are tiny animals sometimes called water bears. They survived 10 days exposed to open space in 2007 (FOTON-M3). ESTABLISHED FACT.

The microbe Methanopyrus kandleri grew at 122 °C under high pressure, as you saw in Deck 20. ESTABLISHED FACT.

Some life doesn't need sunlight at all. Deep-sea vent communities, found in 1977, run on chemical energy, not sunlight. ESTABLISHED FACT. That's a big deal for icy moons: if life on Earth can live in the dark on chemical energy, maybe life could live in a hidden ocean too.

16.text:
Why a G Star Matters

Our Sun is a G star: a middle-of-the-road yellow-white star. It shines steadily for about 10 billion years and peaks in visible light. Photosynthesis on Earth runs on visible light. ESTABLISHED FACT.

K stars (orange dwarfs) are a bit cooler and live longer than the Sun. They may be the best stars of all for life. PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS. M stars (red dwarfs) are more than 75% of stars. They're small and cool and can shine for trillions of years. But their habitable zone is so close that planets there are likely tidally locked, with one side always facing the star. This is expected for close-in planets but not proven for each one: PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

Young M stars blast flares and X-rays for hundreds of millions of years, which may strip the water off planets in the habitable zone. PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS. So is there life around M stars? Proxima b and TRAPPIST-1 e, f and g sit in habitable zones, but nobody knows yet. Webb is checking for air. UNKNOWN.

17.text:
The Best Places Next Door

Habitable means having what life as we know it needs: liquid water, energy and ingredients. Four worlds top the list.

Mars had ancient lakes and has a possible biosignature: PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS. Europa has a salty ocean under the ice: ESTABLISHED FACT. Enceladus has ocean plumes with phosphates and organics: ESTABLISHED FACT. Titan has methane lakes, so life there would need a different chemistry: INFORMED SPECULATION.

18.text:
Europa: An Ocean Under the Ice

Europa is Jupiter's icy moon, a bit smaller than our Moon. Under an ice shell about 15 to 25 km thick is a salty ocean 60 to 150 km deep, with about twice Earth's ocean water. The sizes are estimates, but the ocean is an ESTABLISHED FACT.

Tidal flexing by Jupiter heats the inside and keeps the ocean liquid, like bending a paper clip back and forth until it warms up. ESTABLISHED FACT. Its thin oxygen "air" comes from radiation splitting surface ice, not from life. ESTABLISHED FACT.

Could there be life in cracks in the ice, under the ice, or at seafloor vents? UNKNOWN.

Did you know? NASA's Europa Clipper launched in October 2024 and arrives at Jupiter in 2030.

19.text:
Titan: Life in Methane?

Titan has weather. There's rain, rivers and seas of liquid methane and ethane at about minus 179 °C, under air thicker than Earth's. ESTABLISHED FACT.

That's life not as we know it. Water there is frozen as hard as rock. Life would need a new chemistry, with liquid methane instead of water. INFORMED SPECULATION.

There's even a biosignature to test: methane life might "eat" hydrogen and acetylene. Cassini data (2010) hint that hydrogen vanishes near the surface. But that could be just chemistry, so it's UNKNOWN.

Did you know? NASA's Dragonfly, a flying drone, is set to launch for Titan in 2028.

20.text:
Mars: Leopard Spots

In July 2024, Perseverance drilled the "Sapphire Canyon" sample from a rock called Cheyava Falls. ESTABLISHED FACT. Its spots hold vivianite and greigite, minerals that microbes on Earth help make. ESTABLISHED FACT.

In 2025, a Nature paper called the Cheyava Falls spots a potential biosignature. That means "might be from life, needs more data."

But non-living chemistry can make these minerals too. ESTABLISHED FACT. So did life make them on ancient Mars? UNKNOWN. The best test would be to bring the sample back to labs on Earth.

21.text:
Two Mars False Alarms

Exciting results, then careful re-checks. First, the Viking landers (1976). Mars soil "breathed out" gas when fed nutrients. But almost no organic carbon was found. In 2008, scientists learned that perchlorate in Mars soil can fake the signal. Most say chemistry, so it's UNKNOWN.

Second, meteorite ALH84001 (1996). It's a Mars rock found in Antarctica, with tiny shapes that looked like fossils. But non-living chemistry can make similar shapes and organics. A non-living cause is favored: PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

Both cases show why scientists stay careful before shouting "aliens!"

22.text:
Should We Go There?

Time for space ethics. Agree or disagree? Pick one and defend it with evidence.

Bring Mars rock samples to Earth, even with a tiny risk. Microbes on another world have a right to be left alone. Terraform Mars, even if it turns out to have microbes. Clean every probe carefully, even though it costs more. Send messages to aliens, like Arecibo in 1974, not just listen.

Ask yourself: who decides? What could go wrong? What happens if we DON'T?

Did you know? The Galileo and Cassini spacecraft were crashed on purpose into Jupiter and Saturn so they could never contaminate Europa or Enceladus.

23.text:
Part 3: Searching for Intelligence

Now we go from microbes to minds. Scientists are listening, looking and asking: where is everybody?

If they are out there, why haven't we heard them?

24.text:
Listening and Looking

A technosignature is a sign of technology, not just of life. Radio SETI (since 1960) looks for narrow radio signals that nature doesn't make. There's no confirmed signal so far, and that null result is an ESTABLISHED FACT.

The Wow! signal (1977) was a 72-second radio burst seen at Big Ear, Ohio. It never repeated, and its source is unknown. UNKNOWN.

Optical SETI looks for lasers: very short, very bright flashes. None confirmed: INFORMED SPECULATION. We could also look for pollution in alien air, gases like CFCs that only industry makes. It's an idea to test with big telescopes: INFORMED SPECULATION. Megastructures would show up as starlight blocked or extra infrared heat (see Deck 24): INFORMED SPECULATION.

25.text:
Where Is Everybody?

You met the Fermi paradox in Deck 20: if life is common, why have we found no sign of anyone else? People have proposed plenty of answers.

Rare Earth: Earth needed many lucky conditions, so we may be alone. PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS. Too far or too young: signals haven't reached us, and we've searched very little. PLAUSIBLE HYPOTHESIS.

Great Filter: some step stops most civilizations, maybe one ahead of us. INFORMED SPECULATION. Zoo hypothesis: they see us but choose to stay hidden. INFORMED SPECULATION.

Did you know? Our search so far has been compared to scooping a hot tub's worth of ocean water and expecting to find a fish.

26.text:
How Scientists Test a Claim of Life

The test has five steps. 1, Spot: a possible sign, like a gas, a mineral, a molecule or a signal. 2, Rule out: every non-living way to make it. 3, Repeat: a second instrument or team checks it. 4, Context: does the whole world make sense for life? 5, Return: bring samples to Earth labs if possible.

Cheyava Falls passed step 1; steps 2 and 5 are still open. ESTABLISHED FACT. Viking and ALH84001 stalled at step 2: non-living chemistry can do it. ESTABLISHED FACT. Venus phosphine and K2-18b DMS have not passed step 3 so far. ESTABLISHED FACT.

As Carl Sagan said, extraordinary claims need extraordinary evidence. Your turn: which step did the Wow! signal fail?

27.text:
Student Task: Design a Life-Detection Plan

Now you're the mission scientist. Fill in two parts: A, my target world and why. B, my sign of life and how I rule out fakes.

Pick Mars, Europa, Enceladus, Titan or an exoplanet. Choose one sign of life: a gas, a mineral, a molecule or a signal. List 2 non-living ways it could be made, and how you'd rule them out.

Finally, label each step of your plan on the Evidence Meter. Use Slide 26 as your checklist.

28.text:
Exit Ticket

Show what you learned about life out there.

First, put NASA's definition of life in your own words. Second, name one place life may have started and one problem with it. Third, why are Bennu's amino acids exciting but not proof of life? Fourth, where did the carbon in your body come from? Fifth, back to the hook: which of your "proofs" were only hints, and why?

Then look back at your "I can" list from Slide 3 and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one.

29.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards, plus one science practice. Here's what they ask, in plain words.

ES.2.2: describe the objects in the solar system, like planets, moons, comets, asteroids and protoplanets. Know that planets have been found around other stars, and even drifting with no star. Describe how our solar system is organized. ES.2.3: model the layers and life span of the Sun, and explain how fusion in its core makes elements and energy. It adds that elements heavier than iron form only in supernovae, but scientists now know that about half come from aging giant stars (the s-process) and most of the rest from neutron star mergers and possibly rare supernovae (the r-process).

ES.4.1: build a model of the gases in Earth's air and show how the carbon and oxygen cycles swap gases with living things, oceans, rocks and industry. NGSS Science Practice 7: use evidence to defend or reject a claim, and judge how strong the evidence is.
